subsubtopic: HUMAN RIGHTS ABUSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, May 10, was the anniversary of the independence of Romania, a nation once considered the bread basket of Europe, with a respected cultural heritage.
Today, this country of 23 million is on its knees in the midst of the most severe crisis in its history. Starvation is everywhere. Thousands are imprisoned for their political convictions.
The dictator, Nicolae Ceausescu, is intending to destroy more than 7,000 villages and thousands of churches, cemeteries, and homes. Food, medicine, fuel, and even water are being rationed. Security police are terrorizing the population and those involved in the 1987 riots are still being persecuted. Over 500 people have disappeared.
Europe is incensed and outraged at the disaster zone that is now Romania. Hungary is overflowing with refugees from this cruel regime.
Like many Canadians, we have been increasingly preoccupied by the deteriorating human rights situation in Romania. We must continue to protest these flagrant violations of human rights. I urge the Secretaiy of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to encourage the Romanian Government to co-operate with the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe provisions that were established in Vienna last January.

subtopic: EFFECT OF THE BUDGET ON DAIRY FARMERS
EFFECT OF THE BUDGET ON DAIRY FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, three events in the last five weeks have had an immense impact on the well-being of dairy farmers, including those in Prince Edward Island.
First came the Government's decision to sign the recent GATT Agreement which will freeze industrial milk prices for the next 20 months. This decision disregards a fundamental principle of supply management and goes against a five-year policy commitment that the federal Government made in 1986 to the daily industry.
Then dairy farmers were hit with the elimination of the $7-million subsidy on planned diary export quota, and with a $7-million cut from operation costs of the Canadian Dairy Commission. Together this amounts to an annual loss of $260,000 dollars for the Prince Edward Island dairy farmers.
Time after time, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has insisted that all Canadians must share in the task of controlling our deficit. However, the dairy industry has been asked to do more. This Budget is unfair and unreasonable to diary farmers, in light of the recent GATT Agreements signed by the Government.
May 11, 1989

Mr. Speaker, this week, we are witnessing another adverse effect of the Budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Hundreds of parents from the province of Quebec are threatening to resign from boards of directors of non-profit daycare centres in protest against the potential consequences of the withdrawal by the federal Government of its commitment to child care.
After the Budget announcement, the provinces find themselves with a lot less flexibility for the funding of child care services. In Quebec, the Liberal government is considering cutting back on direct grants to non-profit daycare centres in order to put that money in the only joint funding program maintained by the federal Government, the Canada Assistance Plan. This would cause an increase in the cost of child care services to parents in the province of Quebec.
Where are all those promises that the Conservatives made regarding the support they so wanted to give to parents in Quebec and in all Canada? They have gone up in smoke, and today we are facing an even more severe crisis in the area of child care.

subtopic: NATIONAL FORESTRY WEEK-VALUE OF FOREST RESOURCES
NATIONAL FORESTRY WEEK-VALUE OF FOREST RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, National Forestry Week is an important occasion to remind ourselves about the great value of our forest resources. They are precious to Canadians in many ways: recreational, environmental, and economic.
One impressive measure of the economic value of Canada's forests is the enormous contribution which pulp, paper, lumber, panelboard and a wide range of other forest products make to our international balance of trade.
Based on 1987 statistics from the Canadian pulp and paper industry, Canada exported a total value of $20.3 billion in forest products to other countries. This export
volume is larger than the contribution made by mining, petroleum, fisheries, and agriculture combined.
In economic terms, Canada's forests are the foundation of our enviable position in world trade. For example, one-third of all the pulp and paper sold internationally comes from Canada, and we have customers on every continent, more than 75 countries in all.
Our Government commitment to a strongly mandated Department of Forestry is recognition of the forestry imperative in the Canadian way of life.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY INTO GANDER AIR TRAGEDY

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL INQUIRY INTO GANDER AIR TRAGEDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 12, 1985 at 6.45 a.m. a tragic event occurred in Gander, Newfoundland. An Arrow Airlines DC-8 crashed to the ground killing all people on board. There were 248 American servicemen and eight crew members who lost their lives.
The ensuing investigation by the Canadian Aviation Safety Board has been riddled with controversy and contradiction to such a point that to this day the parents and families of those victims still do not know what caused the deaths of their loved ones.
Later today I intend to table a petition signed by 1,500 Americans who wish a judicial inquiry to take place in order that they can find out the truth about what happened on December 12, 1985 in Gander, Newfoundland.

subtopic: NATIONAL ANTI-DRUG CONFERENCE-RECOGNITION OF WORK OF SELKIRK PRIDE GROUP AND OF DR. IAN REID
NATIONAL ANTI-DRUG CONFERENCE-RECOGNITION OF WORK OF SELKIRK PRIDE GROUP AND OF DR. IAN REID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be part of a Government that recognizes and has declared war on drug abuse.
The community of Selkirk was represented this week at the National Anti-Drug Conference in Saskatoon by Dr. Ian Reid and the Selkirk PRIDE group led by Sharon Purvis. At this conference, the nationally recognized group received an award for being the most active community in Canada for its work in promoting drug abuse awareness. In addition, Dr. Ian Reid received the

May 11, 1989
individual award for his outstanding work in the fight against drug abuse.
I am encouraged by the impact that this group and Dr. Reid are continuing to have on the war against drug abuse, and I salute their efforts.

Mr. Speaker, the week of May 7 to May 13 marks the National Forest Week. Each year, the Canadian Forestry Association bestows on a municipality the title of Forestry Capital of Canada 1989.
I am proud to inform the House that the municipality of La Sarre has been chosen as the Forestry Capital of Canada 1989. La Sarre is the first municipality in Quebec to receive this honour.
This prestigious title will be officially bestowed on the municipality by the Minister of State (Forestry) next Saturday May 13. I am delighted that the people of La Sarre will thus become the focal point of Canada.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate all interested parties as well as all forestry workers in my region whose contribution has made 1989 a memorable year for the municipality of La Sarre.
A big cheer for La Sarre, Forestry Capital of Canada 1989.

subtopic: CLOSURE OF NATIONAL SEA PRODUCTS PLANTS IN ATLANTIC CANADA
CLOSURE OF NATIONAL SEA PRODUCTS PLANTS IN ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement today by Gordon Cummings, the President of National Sea Products Ltd. in Halifax, is another fatal blow to the economy of Atlantic Canada.
National Sea Products Ltd. have closed the Lockeport fish processing plant in Nova Scotia. It is also closing for a two-month period the following fish plants in Atlantic Canada: the Lunenburg wetfish operation, the Canso operation, losing 625 jobs-the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) may laugh, Mr. Speaker, but the people of Atlantic Canada are not laughing. He will have to account for the sins, not only of his Budget, but also because of his fisheries policy which is hurting the people of Atlantic Canada. Stop your smugness and stop your rude remarks.

subtopic: CLOSURE OF NATIONAL SEA PRODUCTS PLANTS IN ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext: Order!

subtopic: CLOSURE OF NATIONAL SEA PRODUCTS PLANTS IN ATLANTIC CANADA
speechtext:
National Sea Products will close the North Sydney fish plant, 400 jobs; Louisbourg in Nova Scotia, 450 jobs; Lockeport, 220 jobs; Burgeo, 450 jobs; Arnolds Cove, 350 jobs; and St. John's, 450 jobs.
I urge the Government of Canada to give a directive to National Sea Products Ltd. to curtail those lay-offs until such time as all the reviews conducted by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans are within the jurisdiction of the Minister.

subtopic: PANAMA-REQUEST FOR CANADA TO SUPPORT REMOVAL OF GENERAL NORIEGA
PANAMA-REQUEST FOR CANADA TO SUPPORT REMOVAL OF GENERAL NORIEGA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the cry for democracy in Panama is being heard throughout the world. The annulment of Sunday's election is nothing less than morally reprehensible and a violation of any notion of justice. The victory by the opposition parties was the first ray of hope for Panamanians to rid themselves of a dictatorship. It was a clear statement for democracy and self-determination. We urge the Government to support the call for General Manuel Noriega's removal from the country, and for the result of Sunday's election to be respected.
The people of Panama have chosen to rid themselves of dictatorship through the democratic process of the ballot box, and they deserve the full support of Canadians. An escalation of violence or militaiy intervention by an outside party at this time would only aggravate the situation and prolong the rule of tyranny. We urge the Government to call in the Panamanian Ambassador and

May 11, 1989

express in the strongest terms possible Canada's rejection of Noriega's hijacking of the will of the Panamanian people.

subtopic: IMPROVED EMPLOYMENT EQUITY FOR THE DISABLED
IMPROVED EMPLOYMENT EQUITY FOR THE DISABLED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you have shown a special interest in the problems which disabled persons face. You will be aware that the recent federal Budget introduced changes in the Income Tax Act which will improve employment equity for disabled persons. They will now be able to deduct the cost of care provided by a part-time attendant to a maximum of $5,000. This initiative, at a revenue cost to the federal Government of $5 million per year, is an important step toward creating equity in the workplace.
This measure is one from a package of tax considerations discussed with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) by the Canadian Paraplegic Association and the Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped, demonstrating that this Government does consult, listen and respond to those deserving equitable treatment.
There remain many other obstacles to full participation of disabled persons in the labour force but I remain confident that this Government is prepared to act and eliminate these obstacles.

Mr. Speaker, while all Canadians are celebrating the National Forestry Week, the people of Jonquiere, the constituency I have the honour to represent in this House, are having problems in a related field, namely with their pulp and paper industry.
Senior executives of Abitibi-Price Inc. met yesterday with the social and economic interest groups of the area and the 1,200 workers of their Kenogami plant.
Mr. Speaker, we don't often see top executives, like Mr. Davis and Mr. Beaudoin, schedule a meeting with
the workers in order to tell them the plant is in trouble. Obviously, the situation is serious.
However, Mr. Speaker, I am sure the workers will be able to face the challenge and to turn their plant into a viable operation in just a few months. It's a huge challenge which the workers will take up with the support of the whole population.

Mr. Speaker, this week we celebrate the Week of the Tree and of the Forests. The slogan "Your Forest and Your Future" illustrates very well the great interest Canadians have in this natural resource, upon which depend close to one million workers. The forest has a national impact, and this is a good opportunity for Canadians to think about its value in our lives.
The ideal thing would be to witness in the coming weeks the renewal of the six federal-provincial agreements on the development of forest resources. They are essential for the viability of the industry and they are in line with the objectives we set for ourselves: to preserve the environment, while at the same time ensuring regional and national economic viability.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, during this Week of the tree and of the Forests, the owners and workers of sawmills across Canada would have been delighted to hear that the 15 percent surtax on lumber exports would be eliminated.

Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of the launching of the campaign to hire students, I would like to urge all the students of my riding looking for a summer job to apply as soon as possible to Canada Employment Centres for Students.
I call on all companies, businesses and private individuals in Drummond, to contribute to the success of the Canada Employment Centre for students by hiring quality manpower.

May 11, 1989
Oral Questions
Through the Challenge '89 program, 302 jobs will be created in my riding, thanks to pay subsidies amounting to $406,314 granted by the federal Government.
I know how much students are counting on those summer jobs and I am particularly proud to contribute to the creation of jobs for the students of Drummondville through this program.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: IMPACT ON MIDDLE-INCOME CANADIANS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Finance could not explain why he violated the principle of universality by attacking old age pensions. Today I want to ask him questions on the disastrous impact of his Budget on the average Canadian.
Can the Minister explain why a two-income family with two children living at the poverty level has seen its taxes rise by 176 per cent, according to his own figures, since he became Minister of Finance? Can he explain why the taxes of a similar family making $100,000 a year have increased by only 11 per cent? Can he explain why taxes paid by families living at the poverty level are growing 16 times faster than those paid by families earning $100,000? Does he think this is fair?

subsubtopic: IMPACT ON MIDDLE-INCOME CANADIANS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to set out very clearly the impact of the tax changes. We acknowledge that there have been tax increases in this Budget. However, I think if the Hon. Leader of the Opposition reflects on what we have done with the large corporations tax, the high income surtax, the number of loopholes that have been changed in the tax system both for corporations as well as for individuals, he will agree that there has been a very substantial
increase in those people with high incomes or corporations that have a better ability to pay the increased tax load. That is the direction we are going. That is clearly the burden of the Budget, and clearly the burden of the changes that we brought in over the past four years.

subsubtopic: IMPACT ON MIDDLE-INCOME CANADIANS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: The questions I have been putting to the Minister over the last two weeks are drawn from his own Budget Papers, all 800 pages of them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to continue the presentation I started this morning on the effect the Budget will have on Canadians. I covered jobs, unemployment, regional development, health, education, and transfer payments.
I would now like to deal with the so-called tax reform promise which raises $3.7 billion or nearly two-thirds of the budget cutting effort. I have a few figures that I would like to pass on for consideration. By 1991 Ottawa will collect $55 billion in personal income tax compared with $29 billion in 1984. This is an increase of close to 90 per cent in seven years. Over the same period total corporate taxes will have increased from $9.4 billion to $14.6 billion. That is an increase of approximately 50 per cent.
In 1965 personal income taxes made up 30 per cent of Canada's revenue and corporate taxes made up 20 per cent. In 1988 the situation had changed. The ratio was personal taxes, 44 per cent; corporate taxes, 11 per cent. For the next three years it is calculated that consumers will continue to pay almost four times as much income
The Budget-Mr. Mifflin
tax as corporations. It is clear that once again individuals are bearing the brunt of the tax load. They are paying more than their fair share. This point was made very adequately by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition about an hour ago in this very Chamber.
On top of this heavy income tax burden there are consumption taxes which will add another $200 to $500 to most family tax bills. The Government has steadily raised consumption taxes in its past Budgets, despite complaints from consumer groups and welfare advocates that such moves penalize the poor. The Government has been unmoved by those arguments.
Householders will also have to shoulder much of the burden of Ottawa's decision to shift the entire funding of unemployment insurance to the private sector. Consumers will probably have to pay higher provincial taxes as a direct result of the lower transfer payments from Ottawa.
Recently the Minister of Finance confirmed that on January 1, 1991 Canadians would begin paying a 9 per cent tax on goods and services, on almost everything but food, rent, health care, and education. In Newfoundland, with 12 per cent provincial sales tax, the net effect will be to add 21 per cent to goods and services at the point of purchase. That is almost 25 per cent on the price quoted in the stores.
This tax started out to be revenue neutral, another catch phrase. I am not sure if it means that the Government will not be collecting more or that the consumer will not be paying more. I do not think the definition matters. Sooner or later, and I would expect sooner, the Government will raise it from 9 per cent to 10 per cent, to 11 per cent, to 12 per cent.
It would be interesting to discuss the experience of some European countries where similar taxes started out at around 10 per cent and in 20 years they were double that amount, around 20 per cent. That works out to approximately half a per cent every year or one per cent every two years. That has us all concerned.
I now wish to turn to the universality of Old Age Security and family allowances. Members of the Government gave repeated personal assurances that universality would continue, would remain, would not be violated, and was a sacred trust. What happened to the sacred trust? This year it will only affect people with an income of $50,000 or more. When will it become $40,000 or $30,000? The foot is in the door. The mind set that universality is here to stay has now been breached. How long will it take? I would suggest that the principle has

May 11, 1989
The Budget-Mr. Mifflin
been established. All we are haggling over now is the price or in this case the threshold.
I do not have very much to say on child care. The Government did not have very much to say on child care. This was another promise close to the heart of Canadians that has been eliminated even before it was put in place.
I have a specific concern pertaining to my riding, which deals with promises, broken promises. In my riding on August 25, 1988 the Government announced approval to construct the first federal penitentiary in Newfoundland. It was a 160-unit medium-minimum security penitentiary, to be constructed at a cost of $30 million. It was to have an annual budget of $7.4 million, and it would employ 100 to 120 people. The prison was to be built in Harbour Grace. I do not have to tell anyone in the House the impact that such an announcement has on a community with a population of approximately 4,000 people.
Harbour Grace? I considered it a living, breathing, real commitment, and so did the people of Harbour Grace.
All Canadians were suitably impressed when the Government stood tall on a promise to continue the effort that was launched in the mid-1970s to improve national defence. There was a White Paper entitled "Challenge and Commitment". Where is that White Paper today? Where is the commitment? Where are the bases that are being closed? Where are the CF-18 replacements? Where is the naval modernization program? What is DND saying to its international colleagues? I would suggest that national defence deserves better. Our men and women in uniform deserve better. Canada deserves better.
This massive tax hike in the Budget, the biggest in Canadian history, will drive up costs and prices and will edge Canada closer to an anticipated economic slowdown. The forecast of the Minister of Finance of an average annual 3.2 per cent rise in real GNP in the next three years is optimistic. Most economists put Canada's potential growth rate in the 1990s at about 2.75 per cent. I understand from economists that this is a tremendous drop.



Twelve days before the November 21 election day there was a sign put up, and here is a shot of it in a local newspaper. It states: "Harbour Grace location of planned federal medium-minimum security penitentiary". That was the sign 12 days before the election. The sign was put up, everyone took note, and everyone made plans. Corrections Canada made plans and the Town of Harbour Grace made plans. What happened to the prison? Something happened, because in the Budget it states: "Construction of the new prison planned for Newfoundland will be delayed, reducing expenditures by $30 million over the next three years. The delay will not jeopardize public safety as existing cell capacity can meet the region's needs".
The Minister for International Trade wrote to the Evening Telegram and stated that he spent three years of continuous work trying to make sure that this prison finally got to Newfoundland some 39 years after Confederation. Can anyone explain what happened to that promise? Can anyone explain that to the people of
Before the Budget was released one-third of Canada's economists were forecasting a recession in the early 1990s as a result of the current high interest rates. Now more than half the economists think that the probability of a recession is more than 50 per cent, and sooner, and that this is a direct result of the Budget.
With some political issues, where one stands often depends on where one sits. That is not the case with this Budget. There is a discomfort index all over the House. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I feel it. It is also felt by my colleagues on this side of the House.
When government members woke up on November 22, and I am winding up my remarks now, they discovered that there was a national debt problem. What is now being proposed as a solution is a disastrous cut in defence spending. Defence represents 10 per cent of government spending, and it is being cut by one-third. There is a reduction in the number of social and regional development programs, and a tax grab that will stifle economic growth and dampen our entrepreneurial spirit for some time to come.

May 11, 1989

In closing, I would like to conclude my remarks by quoting H. L. Mencken who once stated: "Every human problem always has an easy solution-neat, plausible and wrong".

I have a comment and a question for the Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception. I listened with interest to his remarks. When he was talking about the income tax changes, he did not bother to mention the 850,000 low income earners who have been taken off the income tax rolls. When talking about the sales tax, the Hon. Member did not bother to mention the fact that Canadians are now paying a 12 per cent plus sales tax on most of the goods that will be covered in the tax changes. I guess we cannot expect much different. He finally got around to mentioning national defence, but only in the closing moments of his presentation.
I want to make a few comments about national defence with which I am sure the Hon. Member will agree. I believe the biggest threat to Canada's Armed Forces and military effort would be a bankrupt national Treasury. I think the Member realizes that if Canada did not pursue sound economic policies, we would not be able to take our place in the world as a world power and exercise some sort of military intervention when that was required. I cannot believe that he does not recognize the need to trim the budget, to get our financial house in order. I am sure he agrees with us on that point.
How will that be done unless we look at major expenditures like national defence? I am sure the Member, as a military person, does not expect Canada to continue to subsidize military bases simply for the reason of assisting the communities. Surely we can find better methods to provide economic support to Canadian communities.
Is he suggesting that we should keep the trackers in the air for the two hours that they are able to maintain surveillance? Should we retrofit them at great expense to the national Treasury in order to keep what many consider obsolete planes in the air? He is not suggesting that.
My specific question concerns the nuclear propelled submarine issue. We had an address by the Minister of National Defence who explained the Government's
The Budget-Mr. Mifflin
reasoning in this action. I am sure that when the Member remarks on the cut-backs in national defence he will take the nuclear propelled submarines into account.
Did not he, along with his colleagues, complain about the nuclear submarine program during the election campaign? Did he not tell his constituents that it was not necessary and that we should spend the money on child care and social programs?
In the Halifax area candidates said that they did not want nuclear submarines. They said: "We don't want them. We will crush the Navy. We don't care what the future holds for Canada's Navy?
Did the Member join that chorus from the Liberal Party? Was he part of that protest movement? Did he cause Canadians to rise up against the nuclear submarine acquisition so that the people demanded the cancellation of that program? Was he part of that?

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted at the number of questions put to me by the Hon. Member for Halifax West. I am not sure where to begin.
Some suggestions were made across the floor. I remind the House that I was privy to a lot of information that caused national defence to be where it is today.
The House will be aware that the acquisition program of ships, aircraft and tanks takes anywhere from eight to twenty years. I recall distinctly a cabinet memorandum and a paper which was initiated by the Liberal Party. I can even remember the date, December 22, 1977. That was a great day because the Liberal Party, the Government of the day, decided that Canada should have 24 frigates to make up a strong Navy. That was the position of the Liberal Party in 1977. It was the position of the Liberal Party as we commissioned six that are built and six more that are being built. It will continue to be the position of the Liberal Party. We support a very strong Navy. I am for a strong Navy, and I can assure the House that every member in the Liberal Party on this side of the House is for a strong Navy.
There are other aspects of this which I would be quite prepared to address. However, I want to return to something my hon. friend from Halifax West said about whether I remembered the low income Canadians who are not taxed. Does he remember the high income Canadians who are not paying much tax?

May 11, 1989
The Budget-Mr. Mifflin
I am sure there are other questions, so I will wait for them.

The Hon. Member can correct me if I am wrong, but I understand that he was in the Armed Forces and served this country well and honourably. We as Canadians appreciate that very much.
How can he stand up in the House today and talk about the defence of this nation after what the Government has done over the last five years for the Armed Forces, compared to what Prime Minister Trudeau and his merry band of bandits did to the Armed Forces during the period he governed this country? Now he stands up in the House to say with emotion and fervour that the Armed Forces are being destroyed. It is to maintain a good, solid Armed Forces and to provide the equipment that the men and women of the Armed Forces deserve. Why did he not stand up and speak about that when he was in the Armed Forces?

I come here to serve as a politician. Only two years ago the defence White Paper entitled "Challenge and Commitment" gave great hope to this country with a commitment to continue the modernization process that was begun earlier by the Liberals in the mid-1970s.
Let me answer the Minister's question. It would appear from the lead up announcements to the Budget that the Minister of National Defence must have agreed to a series of cuts or delays in major capital acquisition programs, in a real effort to save the nuclear submarine program. It appears equally likely that the change of mind centred on the Government's inability to sell a tough Budget if this high profile, increasingly nationally unpopular project was left unscathed. DND got the worst of both worlds. It got both barrels-bang, bang.
The spending cuts leave national defence in tatters. Will the capital acquisition delays result in equipment rust out? Will the manpower cut-backs leave the forces unable to meet the White Paper manpower commitment to NATO and to reinforce Europe? What is the rethinking on redressing the balance to have a strong Navy and the new approach to ensuring Canadian Arctic sovereignty? Where is that vigorous naval modernization program Canada was embarking upon?
What about base closings? They will cost jobs and decimate the local economies of regions across Canada. They will decrease our mobility infrastructure.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise in the House today to speak to this Government's budgetary policy.

I have been following the debate closely. I want to use this opportunity to address one or two specific misconceptions about the Budget. Before I do that, however, I want to look at the entire Budget.
In this debate we have heard a great deal-and we heard it just now again-about the negativism that delights in picking holes in the details of policy, especially policies that show a breath of vision. Speaker after speaker from the other side has avoided dealing with the overriding imperative that has shaped the Finance Minister's Budget-Canada's large and growing public debt.
We have heard them criticize the Government and what it is trying to do to get the burgeoning debt under control. They have criticized every single budget cut that the Government has announced-every single one. We just had a member of the Liberal Party criticize the decision on the nuclear propelled subs.
They have criticized every single budget cut. They have criticized every single tax increase. There has not been one that they have not criticized.
However, what they have not done is they have not been honest with the Canadian people. They have not stood up in their places and said where they would cut, where they would save money for the Government, where they would try to get the debt under control, where they would try to get the deficit down-not once. Not one Member has said that.
I sat and listened to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) ad nauseam the other day. He criticized every single part of the Budget. However, did he have any ideas as to how to get the debt under control? Not one.
Do you remember, Mr. Speaker, when he ran in 1984? He was going to cut the deficit in half in a very few years. He did not say how. Then, in 1988, he said: "By golly, that did not work in 1984. Cutting the deficit did not work in 1984 so in 1988 I am going to make $40 billion worth of promises in the campaign. That is what I am
The Budget-Mr. McDermid
going to do". His whole caucus, this fine looking group of men and women, together with their socialist buddies, have stood up time after time and criticized. However, they have not had one idea.
Do you know what they say, Mr. Speaker? It happened just the other day. They sat there and they yelled at me the other day. They said: "It is not our problem, no, no, no. It is your problem. You are the Government. You solve the problem. Do not ask us for ideas".
The Hon. Member who is a former Cabinet Minister and who has a new riding now-it is South West Nova-sat there the other day and said: "It is not my problem. The debt, the deficit are not my problem". I am going to tell you, Mr. Speaker, it is everybody's problem.

speechtext:
Let me review how the problems developed.

May 11, 1989
The Budget-Mr. McDermid
Some 20 years ago Canada had no deficit. Our total debt at that time was $18 billion. The debt was $18 billion but there was no deficit. In other words, we were bringing in enough income to pay for that debt without having to borrow to pay for it.
At that time 12 cents of every revenue dollar-every dollar that the Government collected in taxes-every dollar my friend the tax collector collected-I mean the Minister of Revenue, who is sitting here in front of me today-went into interest payments. That was 20 years ago. Four and a half years ago, when this Government came to office, that debt had grown to nearly $200 billion. The amount of revenue devoted to the interest payment on that debt had grown to 32 cents out of every dollar. The annual deficit that year was $38 billion. In one year it was $38 billion.
This dramatic increase, as I said earlier, should be of concern to all Members. For now we have a self-propelling force in our public finances that threatens to undermine our reputation for fiscal prudence and responsibilities. We must bring that debt under control so that we can maintain this nation's ability to provide the social programs, the Armed Forces and the services that Canadians value and rely upon.
Let me be more precise about the burden that debt imposes on our Government's financial flexibility. In 1988-89, $33 billion was spent on public debt charges, that is, just the interest on the existing debt. That makes debt interest payments the biggest single category of government spending.
I would ask Hon. Members to keep in the back of their minds that we are paying $33 billion. I would like to compare that with transfers to persons. We do a great number of transfers to persons here with the funding we collect. Transfers to persons this year is $30 billion. The interest on the public debt alone costs us more than Old Age Security, the Guaranteed Income Supplement, family allowances and veterans' pensions all together. For the current year we forecast that the debt will rise to $39.4 billion. That is the interest on the debt. This year 35 cents out of every revenue dollar will go to pay interest on the public debt.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, what a Government could do if it had that 35 cents and did not have to pay interest on this huge debt that we have? Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, what services we could provide or
what taxes we could cut? Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, what income we could leave in the pockets of the people of Canada?
That is the problem. It is so clear that we cannot continue to pay more and more of every revenue dollar on debt interest and still be able to provide the services that, let us face it, Canadians now take for granted. Health care is one, as are old age pensions and so on. Beginning in 1987-88, and carrying on into 1988-89, public debt charges have exceeded the annual deficit. In other words, without our large stock of debt we would have a budgetary surplus in each year. We would have a budgetary surplus if we did not have to pay the interest on this huge debt.
This has put us on a treadmill. It has become a major problem because now we are just borrowing money to pay interest. That is insane. There is no end to that. That is why the Minister of Finance brought in the Budget he did. I would like to tell you something. Nobody on this side of the House likes this Budget. That is why I agree with what is going on over there.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nobody likes it. We do not like raising taxes. We do not like cutting spending but we know that it is needed. If we do not do it now, within the next two or three years we will be spending 50 cents of every $1 collected just to pay the interest. This Government has the guts to come to grips with the problem. Opposition Members have no guts at all. They do not have any idea how to handle this problem.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are they bankrupt?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, they are bankrupt of ideas. They have not made one suggestion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They run their Party like they ran the country.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is right. Yes, I believe their Party is still in debt quite a bit. That is the way that they ran this Government for a number of years too.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No wonder we are in trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What has been going on is that total spending on Government has dropped significantly as a portion of national income. Over the last four years, the Minister of Finance has made sure that program spending has only grown at an average of 3.6 per cent a year,
May 11, 1989

which is less than the rate of inflation. Actually, it is less than half the growth in the economy.
Over that period, costs of Government operations have actually fallen. The costs of operating the Government, not the transfers of moneys to provinces, medicare or to people; whatever it may be, but the cost of actually operating the Government, which is about 16 per cent of our total expenditures, has gone down over the last four years. We have trimmed and we have reduced the annual deficit. It has dropped from 8.6 per cent of GNP, when we took over, to 4.8 per cent in 1988-89. It dropped to $28.9 billion in the fiscal year just ended. That is almost $9.5 billion below the level of what it was when we took over in 1984. However, it is not enough. We have to do more. The measures introduced in the present Budget take us further along the path of fiscal responsibility, the path we have been on since we came to office. The measures reflect the seriousness of the present situation. They are a result of a great deal of work, and some tough decisions.
I sat with the Minister of Finance, along with my colleague, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Loi-selle), and our Parliamentary Secretary, and he can tell you the tough decisions that had to be made. I would like to say that paramount in our Minister of Finance's mind in all of those deliberations, was to make sure that the less fortunate in our society were protected.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was paramount in the deliberations that went on for this Budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Breath-taking.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is my jolly friend from Edmonton, the token socialist from Alberta, chuckling away in the back row. He was not here when his Leader stood up in the House after the Minister of Finance delivered his economic statement in November of 1984 and predicted the greatest doom and gloom for this country. Two hundred thousand jobs were going to be lost-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Two hundred and fifty thousand.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Two hundred and fifty thousand, was it? Two hundred and fifty thousand jobs were going to be lost, and we were going into a recession as a result of this economic statement and the role that the Government had taken. This is how accurate he is every time he
The Budget-Mr. McDermid
stands up and makes a prediction. I turn him right off because he has been wrong every time.
In the next four years a million and a half jobs were created, a million and a half more people are paying taxes, and have worth-while, meaningful jobs. That is what has happened because of the economic guidance we have given this country.
In the few minutes left to me I would like to turn to some criticisms that have been expressed in this debate which I think are unfair. First, one of the things that the Opposition Parties have been saying all along is that this Budget is an attack on families. This is what they state: It is an attack on families. Let me tell you what an attack on families is. The minute a baby is bom in this country-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You tax it.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-that child owes $12,000. Every day that child lives that debt goes up $3. That is an attack on the families. That child and that child's child cannot be paying our debts. That is why we have tried to come to grips with the debt problem and the deficit problem in this country.
I ask the critics to be realistic. The real threat to families is the growing debt. There is no question about that. Without action to control it, our flexibility to take action is constrained by the debt charges.
That has never been discussed by the Members opposite. They have never stood up and said: "Hey, we do have a problem here. We should do something about it. Here is what we propose". Not one of their speakers have done that. I have listened to the whole debate and read the debate, and none of them have done that. The NDP Party says that it has. It said, "bring the Armed Forces back from Europe and that will save money".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

May 11, 1989
The Budget-Mr. McDermid
corporations that are not paying taxes. The NDP Party is always exaggerating. I have told the Members a million times, "do not exaggerate".

The measure is progressive. It affects only 14 per cent of the present recipients of family allowance. Less than 10 per cent will end up paying back all of their family allowance. If I ever had a suggestion from the public presented to me more on debt reduction, it was this one: that family allowances should be taxed back from the high income people. That was suggested to me many, many times. I know that my friend from Kingston and the Islands (Mr. Milliken) heard that suggestion from his constituents as well. It is the same with the old age security, there is no question about that.
Mr. Speaker, I notice you are signalling me but I still have time. I watched my hon. friend give his speech and he received about an extra seven minutes-

speechtext: Order, order.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would hope that there might be a little leeway in the Chair.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Time. Time.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In any event, Mr. Speaker, our agenda has always been open.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was well hidden.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It has always been clear, right from 1984, day one, when the Minister of Finance presented his economic statement. It was just not talked about, but proclaimed in that economic statement of 1984 and reaffirmed explicitly in budget after budget and in throne speeches. It was discussed-I get this-we did not discuss it in the last election. I would like to tell you what
happened when I got into all candidate meetings in the last election. I started talking about the deficit. My opponents stood up and said, "You are afraid to debate free trade. You are getting off the subject. We want to talk about free trade. We do not want to talk debt. We do not want to talk deficit". That is what went on in the last election.
I am going to conclude with this: If we are going to maintain the social, cultural and other programs that are an integral part of Canada, if we are going to meet the needs of the people of Canada who need the help most, then we must have an efficient and effective government. We must have a balanced and equitable financial system. We must get out from under this crushing load of debt and get it under control.
I believe the Budget presented by my colleague is an important one for Canada. It builds on what has gone on before. It addresses the problems we face today. It sets out a reasonable set of measures which will enable us to deal with the debt problem and, at the same time, preserve our social programs. I am proud to be able to stand and register my support for it and for the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the speech I now understand fully what Amnesty International means when it refers to cruel and unusual punishment. I do not envy you having to listen to several Tories across the way. Being the non-partisan person that you are, that must be real punishment.

We would cut spending. We would not raise taxes. rIax levels in

May 11, 1989

Liberals have made election promises. Conservatives have made spending commitments-In the way that I have described it, yes, it is zero (the cost of Tory election promises) -.In those reserves, we have sufficient money to handle the announcements that we made prior to the election and those that have been made since the election was called.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

We achieved this record (of deficit reduction) with a new disciplined approach to the management of government and its expenditures.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Wreck the family.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party

Let me see. I have got another one here and it is even better.
In the future, Canada will be doing more, not less for all of you. As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada, social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished by our Government -
I guess it is a give-away right there, Mr. Speaker. That was the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on October 15, 1988, in Summerside, Prince Edward Island.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is terrible.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I know it is extremely unfair to quote the Prime Minister using his own words, but does the Minister across the way remember those words from the last election campaign? If so, could he explain today why this double-speak and this double-talk on the part of Tories should be endured by any Canadian?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that Canadian people are smarter than the Hon. Member opposite. Canadians are beginning to understand the problems we have in this country. They understand why we are trying to do something about it. Do you know something? I
The Budget-Mr. Harvey
think they are prepared to support this Government in trying to tackle this problem. They are far more committed, far more interested than the Opposition Parties are in this problem. I do not think there is any question about that. The Prime Minister said that social benefits will be improved. To my recollection this year senior citizen's pensions will be raised four times and about 4.9 per cent.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Clawed back.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Here is my hon. friend saying, "Claw back", whatever that means. What we are doing is exactly what his Party asked us to do and that is tax those in the higher income brackets. The Hon. Member is defending people earning over $75,000 a year. That is what he is doing now. The Leader of the Opposition said, and I heard him say it many times, "Tax those in the high income area". That is what we are doing with this Budget. Members of the NDP have said the same thing, "Tkx the rich". It was their campaign, tax the rich. That is exactly what is done in this Budget. Four per cent of senior citizens earning over net $50,000, which works out to about $60,000 or $70,000, somewhere in there, will pay taxes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Universality.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is universality. They get their cheques, and it is taxed back, and that is the answer. Yes, our Prime Minister said social benefits will be improved, and they are being improved. There is no question about it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not to our seniors.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every speech I have heard from across the way during the course of this debate has at some point or another included a statement to the effect that the Opposition has advanced not a single idea on how we might come to grips with the deficit and the debt. I must say if that were that the case, I would, in fact, be truly ashamed and I would feel myself compelled not to rise in this debate.
However, I know that even before the Minister's Budget was-well, I was going to say presented-our finance critic had sent to the Minister of Finance a six-page letter detailing a dozen proposals for various budgetary programs that could be used to reduce the deficit and begin to tackle the debt, including six proposals dealing with taxes alone.

The Budget-Mr. Milliken
I understand, and we have had it demonstrated in the last week, that communication within the Ministry is not the most efficient. It is possible that the Finance Minister neglected to share these excellent ideas with his colleagues, both within the Ministry and within his Party. I have a copy for the Hon. Minister. In fact, I have copies for any of the unfortunately benighted Members of the benches opposite.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Table it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry, I have not sufficient copies to table. We work on restricted budgets over here.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will just send this over to the Minister, and while it is in transit, might I ask him whether we are really to take seriously his protestations of fairness in the matter of taxes in the Budget? His Government's record, not according to the NDP, but according to the Institute for Research on Public Policy; in the course of this Government's first mandate, for the richest 1 per cent of Canadians, the tax burden was reduced by $3,500 a year, while everyone else's went up. Are we to place the slightest shred of credibility then in the taxation policies of this Government?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I get a charge out of the New Democrats and the various Budgets they talk about. For example, the Hon. Member is talking about tax. He is talking about tax reform a year or so ago when we reduced something like nine or ten different tax levels to three tax levels. The NDP forget that. The Government took 850,000 low-income earning Canadians off the tax rolls. These Canadians do not pay taxes anymore. The Hon. Member fails to mention that. He fails to mention that this Budget increased taxes for high-income people. He forgets to mention that the wealthy in this country who have more ability to pay got an extra surcharge, and we have heard from them too.
The Hon. Member talks about corporations. One of the things the New Democrats do not understand, and they showed their ignorance when they were debating the Free Trade Agreement, Canada is a trading nation. We rely on 30 per cent of our income in this country, three million jobs, many of them unionized, on international trade. If we cannot be competitive with those countries we are trading with, then we will not do any
trading. This gang of bandits would tax these corporations right out of existence because if we followed their tax recommendations and policies, the companies could not compete in the world of trade today, and that is a fact.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is blackmail.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Hon. Member is yelling "blackmail". That shows the absolute ignorance of that Party when it comes to international trade and its importance to Canada. The Hon. Member should talk to some union members, particularly those in my community who work in the auto trade. He would find out how competitive they have to remain if they want to sell their products to the United States.
Any company that trades has to be competitive. If we tax them out of existence, they will not be competitive. That is the NDP philosophy, and I understand it.
Perhaps the Hon. Member should take time to study this Budget. He would see that high income earners will be paying proportionately more. He will see that the
850,000	who were dropped off the tax rolls are still off the tax rolls. He will see that there was a doubling of the sales tax credit to low income earners. If he did that, maybe then he would be honest with the Canadian people when he criticizes. Perhaps he would be a little more objective.

Mr. Justice William Henderson, as he now is, of the Ontario Supreme Court, served as a Member in this House for many years. The Hon. Flora MacDonald who for 16 years represented the riding in this House and served her country as Secretary of State for External Affairs, Minister of Employment and Immigration, and Minister of Communications. In addition, Kingston boasts a series of penal institutions, and in many ways it is the penal capital of Canada, having more prisons within the confines of the riding than almost any other place. Member for Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Vankoughnet).
In addition, Kingston has a substantial military base which, fortunately, has not been closed by this Budget.
The Budget-Mr. Milliken

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are lucky.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are lucky, very lucky. In addition, it has many industries that are well known across Canada and are part of national chains, as well as many smaller businesses that flourish in the community.
Kingston is one of Canada's oldest communities. It was founded in 1673 by le comte de Frontenac and has survived to this day. It is of course known as the Limestone City because of its many beautiful limestone buildings. Kingston is active in preserving its historic past. There are active historical societies that seek to preserve the ancient buildings of Kingston and make use of them for future generations by maintaining them in good condition.
The riding itself comprises the City of Kingston, the Township of Kingston, part of the Township of Pittsburgh, and the three townships that comprise the islands of the riding-Wolfe Island, Howe Island, and Amherst Island. These three islands sit off the south shore of the mainland of Ontario in the St. Lawrence River very close to our boundary with the United States.
Kingston is Canada's second largest retirement centre after Victoria and has a substantial population of seniors. Those people, I must say, are disappointed with the Budget that we are discussing today. I would like to turn now to that Budget.
The Minister of State for Privatization (Mr. McDer-mid) was on his feet immediately before me and gave what I can only describe as an incredible speech. He was shedding crocodile tears about how he hated, as he maintained did everyone on that side of the House, to impose taxes. Honestly we have never had a Government that has imposed taxes the way this Government has. For him to make that rather bold-faced statement and try to maintain that it was an accurate representation of the true feelings of the Government is, quite frankly, unbelievable.
I would like to turn to the attack that has been made on the universality of social programs by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in this Budget. I want to deal specifically with seniors, because recently they have decided that it is time to speak out and condemn the Government for the actions it has taken. There is an article in today's The Ottawa Citizen in which the National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation is quoted. It has launched its criticism of this Budget. The group sent telegrams, The Ottawa Citizen reports, to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and to the Minister of Finance

May 11, 1989
The Budget-Mr. Milliken
on Wednesday protesting the claw-back program the Government has embarked upon. The article quotes the group as saying:
"We think we were betrayed because both the prime minister and the Minister of Finance - indicated there would be no tampering with the social security programs,"- "Seniors were misled by statements that were made during the election".

I would like to remind Hon. Members opposite who seem to have forgotten that citizens contributed to their pensions for many years. Having made that contribution, I find it incredible that today, they are not receiving those benefits. They receive them only to pay them all back.
The Minister of State for Privatization tried to justify this move by saying that they were simply taxing the rich, but the only rich that are being taxed by this scheme are the the seniors who are receiving a pension. I suggest that that is unfair-
