I will argue it with the Hon. Member any day. It is a tax of 100 per cent.
I am sorry to keep drawing attention to the Minister of State for Privatization, but after all, it was his speech that immediately preceded mine. He stood there and complained, as the Minister of Finance whines and complains every day in Question Period, that we never come up with any suggestions for saving money, that we always criticize every cost cutting measure that Hon. Members opposite propose.
We have praised the nuclear submarine cuts. I have another suggestion for the Hon. Members opposite that will save us a good deal of money. They should abandon the rather stupid advertising campaigns to which they are subjecting Canadians as a result of this Budget. Over $2.7 million has been wasted to convince Canadians that the national debt is a problem. How stupid can they get? Honestly, if the Government is going to waste the money of Canadians in this way, surely it should not be complaining about us saying "don't cut here and don't cut there".
We are trying to save programs that mean something to Canadians, not wasting money on advertising in newspapers, on radio and on television trying to tell Canadians that the debt is a particular problem. If Canadians cannot understand that the debt is a problem, they should leave it and deal with it in the Budget. That is what they have done. We do not need a huge advertising campaign with the pictures of loonies with the sides cut out of them to illustrate that the debt is a particular problem. That is an example of waste of money.
In fact, the Government is spending over $90 million a year trying to convince Canadians that its policies are right. Canadians know they are wrong. They do not need to be convinced with ads. I would suggest that the Government pull that advertising campaign at once and save Canadians some of their money. There is a suggestion. Do not let me hear again that there has never been a suggestion from this side on how to save money. I will come up with another if I am forced to.
I have got another way to save money, that is, to cut down the size of Cabinet. We have never had such a huge Cabinet in Canadian history. It has continued from 1984. If this Government were serious about saving money, it would cut down the numbers of members of its Cabinet and save all those salaries and car allowances. There has been no suggestion that there will be any cuts

there. It has been left intact. It is a huge Cabinet, oversized, and, as we saw earlier today, sadly lacking in competence.
I would like to turn to a couple of other items in this Budget that I think are particularly unfair. I would like to turn to the proposed cuts in VIA Rail, a most shocking breach of promise on an absolutely grand scale. Here we have a Government, as I indicated in a comment the other day, that came into office in 1984 promising, with solemn promises by the Deputy Prime Minister in particular, that it would restore VIA Rail to its former grandeur and make it a show case of railway travel for the world right here in Canada. Every single line was going to be improved. The Minister reinstated lines that had been cut and said that they could not do without them and that they were vitally important to our country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We found out later that we could not afford to do those things when you guys left.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We could afford it in 1984 while you were doubling the debt and now you are telling us that we cannot afford it because you have doubled it already. The deficit is going up and up.
The behaviour of Hon. Members opposite is so inconsistent that it borders on the ludicrous. The Hon. Member laughs; she should be ashamed of the Government that she is supporting. These cuts to VIA Rail fly completely contrary to the promises made by the Deputy Prime Minister and many other members of the Cabinet opposite. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg South interrupts and suggests that I am not being fair in my comments, but I tell her that I am being perfectly fair in my comments. They are accurate. She should pay more attention to the facts.
Another thing I would like to turn to deals with VIA Rail and the proposed cuts. These continual reductions over a four-year period will have a devastating effect on this company. In 1987 VIA Rail paid $179 million in trackage fees to CN and to CP. Last year it paid $103 million for the privilege of using those tracks. VIA Rail was created in order to save those two companies money, one of which is wholly owned by the Government, CN. In fact, its President has been appointed head of VIA Rail.
Those companies have these tracks, and they were relieved of their obligation to run passenger service so that they could make more money, in both cases. They
The Budget-Mr. Milliken
applied to the Canadian Transport Commission to have their obligation to carry passengers lifted so that they did not have to lose money on passenger service. The Government of the day created VIA Rail to take that particular service out of those two railways and put it in a new corporation, VIA Rail, where the operation would be carried on.
VIA pays $100 million to subsidize the maintenance of tracks on those railways. It was created for the sole purpose of preventing them from losing money on passenger service. I suggest that they should be getting that service for free. Instead of cutting the operation grants, the Government should introduce legislation to say that they get it for free. Then there would not be a need to cut the operating grants because $100 million would be saved right off. That is more than is being cut this year.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg South shakes her head. I say to her "go and look at the facts". Canadians have built the national train service. We have paid for it over the years. It was a precondition of the establishment of this country that we have a rail line to British Columbia. Now this Government is seeking to destroy our railway system. I say that is wrong, that is improper, and that the Government ought not to be doing it. The largest committee room in this building, as far as I know, is the Railway Committee Room behind us. It was called such because of the massive amount of time Parliament has spent on railways over the years. Now, with a stroke of a pen, the Minister of Finance says that they are going to carve up VIA Rail, cut it out, sell it off, sell off chunks of the service, sell off lines here and there, get the provinces to operate it, and shift the expense and the burden to somebody else. The Minister is incompetent to organize the finances of Canada in such a way-and he has had five years to do it-that that burden can be properly shouldered by the people of Canada today. That is the problem.
The question of child care is another one that I would like to address. I recall during the last campaign how much we heard about child care, how important it was, and how frightful it was that the other place had held up the child care legislation. Let us see the record in this regard. I am sick and tired of listening to this drivel. I heard it all through the election from my opponent.
The child care Bill was passed in this House on September 26, 1988. It went to the Senate for first

May 11, 1989
The Budget-Mr. Milliken
reading on September 27. It was called for second reading on September 28 and got through second reading. Parliament was dissolved two days later, on September 30. Yet the Minister of Finance has the gall to stand up and say that this was held up by the Senate. It was four days in the Senate, and we are told that the reason we do not have the child care Bill passed today is that the Senate held it up. That is just rubbish.
The Senate was not taking an undue amount of time on this. The Senate offered to stay in session for another day in order to pass this Bill, but the Prime Minister would not have it. He said: "No, no. We are going to the people. We are going to dissolve Parliament". He kept saying all through the campaign that we would have had child care if it were not for the Senate. We now see that in fact that was not accurate. He misled Canadians during the election.
The Minister of Finance stood up the other day and said that we could not have child care because we could not afford it. If we cannot afford it today, why could we afford it in October or November? He did not want to admit that we could not afford it. It was a complete deception of the Canadian people. They were not told the facts. The Minister of Finance knows it, the Prime Minister knows it, and I suggest that his supporters know it.
I would like to turn to CIDA because this has to be one of the most vicious and nasty cuts that we have seen in this whole Budget. CIDA's grants and contributions are being cut by $200 million. That in itself is appalling, but I suggest that what is worse is the increase in the costs of operating CIDA. They have gone up by $19 million-$19 million extra to administer $200 million less. It is a shocking indictment of the priorities of this Government-cut aid to Third World countries and increase the payments to the people who administer the funds. That is what is going on in these Estimates. The Hon. Member should read the Estimates. I refer her to page 9-3 of the Estimates that were tabled in this House. It is completely shameful. The Hon. Member should read the Estimates.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are misleading the people of Kingston.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I invite the Hon. Member to read the Estimates.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope they do not listen to you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope that they do not listen to the Minister of Finance. The stories of misleading and intellectual dishonesty during the last campaign are coming to light every day in the House with new revelations of incompetence and new stories of financial horror the Minister of Finance conjures up in order to convince Canadians that what he is doing is right.
The final statement in the Budget must be for Canadians to look at the amount of tax increases and then look at the amount of cuts. The deficit has increased; it has not gone down. It has increased, despite this huge tax increase. I suggest that the reason it has increased so much is that government spending is out of control. In spite of the announced big cuts in defence, and in spite of the big cuts to CIDA, and the nasty tax back on Old Age Security earners, the Government has failed in its attempts to bring the deficit under control. It has failed to convince Canadians that what it is doing is right. I suggest that it has done the opposite and convinced Canadians that it is unfit to remain in office.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I congratulate the Hon. Member opposite, my erstwhile travelling companion, on his fine maiden speech which was very well done. The Hon. Member certainly gave us an interesting piece of history. He suggested to us that we should continue to subsidize VIA Rail because the nation was built on the promise of a railroad from coast to coast.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That's right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am questioning his logic. Is the Hon. Member suggesting that we should also continue to use the horse and buggy, because traditionally this country was built on that type of mode of power?
We heard from the Hon. Member opposite a litany of complaints about cut-backs. He also suggests that government spending is out of control. However, the Hon. Member does not seem to have any concrete suggestions for how we can fund some of the programs that he holds so dear to his heart. He made some casual suggestion about cutting some advertising program. However, he has not offered one item of real substance.
May 11, 1989

Could the Hon. Member explain to us his program to reduce the debt and the deficit? Perhaps the Hon. Member could give us an outline of his program.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thought I had given some ideas to the Hon. Member. I suggested to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg South that the advertising budget of the Government be cut. The Hon. Member should use her influence with the Ministers in front of her to do this. If she has been attempting to do so, I believe the pleas have fallen on deaf ears.
I thank the Hon. Member for her question and comment. The Hon. Member knows as well as I do that she has a duty to represent her constituents. I would like to know their views on the cuts to VIA Rail. Do they know that the Hon. Member is supporting this scheme to slash VIA?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, they do. I am encouraged.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad that she encourages them to buy up these cuts. I have a feeling that, come the next election, they may remember her support and may have something to say to her about her chances of being re-elected.
Every Member on the other side of the House, including the Minister of Finance, whines and whimpers that we are not suggesting ways to cut. When we suggest ways, they are ignored. Today I have made two very sound suggestions to save millions of dollars, and there has been no positive response from the other side. I do not know why the Minister of Finance does not run down from his office now and say: "Yes, all right, we will cut the $92 million from advertising". We have suggested something, and I do not know why he does not come down and agree. Instead there is dead silence, and all we get is a statement that we have not suggested anything.
We are not the Government. We are the Opposition.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is a very good reason.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It will not be for long. I can tell Hon. Members that there is no need for us to come up with all the suggestions to help them run the Government. That is not our job. Our job is to look at the proposals they make and ask if those proposals are fair and just in the eyes of the people of Canada. I have stated that the proposals the Government has made are unfair and unjust. They are discriminatory in that they are taxing the senior citizens of the country, the people who have
The Budget-Mr. Young
worked and contributed to the schemes that we have in place. Those are the people the Government is depriving of money, and I suggest that that is unfair. Our job is as an Opposition. The Government's job is to propose, and our job is to oppose.
However, I have come up with suggestions that are falling on deaf ears. Hon. Members opposite are so enamoured of their misguided proposals that they feel to convince the Canadian people of how good these misguided proposals are that they have to advertise and put it all through the papers. There is $90 million worth of advertising to convince Canadians about the wrong policies that are being pursued.
If the policies were correct, there would be no need to advertise. Perhaps that is why we have to go through the charade of spending $90 million to convince Canadians. Perhaps that is why we need so many members of Cabinet. There have to be more spokesmen to sell a bad policy than to sell a good policy. We on this side of the House are selling good policies to Canadians.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have a question for the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands. I too wish to congratulate him on his maiden speech.
I wonder if the Member would agree that the Government seems to have something against pensioners. I do not know what its hang up is, but it has something against pensioners. The Hon. Member may recall, even though he was not in the House, that the Minister of Finance, when he was attempting to defend his proposal to deindex pensions in the 1985 Budget when speaking to the Chamber of Commerce in Montreal, made the statement that he did not think there were enough rich people in Canada, and this was why he was attempting to deindex old age pensions. We all know that the Minister has been preoccupied.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A little bit of honesty.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Did the Hon. Member say "lies"?
In the last four years the Government has consistently attacked pensions. There is no question about that, and it is doing so again.
My question for the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands is the following one. In establishing government priorities, surely to goodness the Government should be aware that there has been an explosion in the number of food banks across the country. The Canadian

May 11, 1989
The Budget-Mrs. Gibeau
Association of Food Banks released a press release today pointing out this very fact.
In terms of establishing priorities, surely Government has an obligation to say to people who are living in abject poverty that it wants to do something for them, rather than the 60,000 very profitable corporations that ain't paying a red cent in income tax. That is the type of priority the Government should be addressing, and it is not.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course, I agree with the comment made by the Hon. Member. It is accurate. Hon. Members opposite laugh when they hear the facts. Seniors are being very badly treated in the Budget. The record of the Government is a very dismal one in respect to seniors. Perhaps Hon. Members opposite represent suburban areas of Canada and not the downtown areas that some Members here represent. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg South is a prime example. We know about the problems faced by those people who are deprived of a livelihood by the Government with these vicious taxes.
I wish to turn to another matter, but I do not wish to provoke Hon. Members opposite too much. However, during the election campaign my Conservative opponent was a person very near and dear to the hearts of Hon. Members opposite. During an all-candidates debate she was discussing the fact that the Conservative promises made during the election were not going to cost Canadians a cent and that it was all looked after in the financial plan of the Government. I asked if it was not in the Budget and she turned to me and said: "Peter, you don't understand government finance".
I understand government finance. I understand that to pay for these promises, the ones that are not broken, we are seeing another huge tax increase in Canada. The seniors are being taxed to the hilt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Seniors are not being taxed to the hilt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is taken out of their limited incomes by the new sales tax. That is how the Government is paying for those promises. That is the financial plan of the Government. The financial plan always was to hike taxes and use the additional money to pay for the promises it chose not to break. It is a shocking record of financial organization and mismanagement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mrs. Gibeau).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today on behalf of my constituents in Montreal North- Bourassa to support the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). When I talk to people in my riding, to men and women representing various interest groups, to my friends and family, they all say I am concerned about so many issues: the environment, health care, ageing of the population, immigration, the declining birth rate, and especially Canada's debt. And the last one is very important. How not the Government, but our society deals with these issues will determine the quality of life in Canada in the years to come. Today, I want to say to my constituents in Montreal-North- Bourassa that our Government not only listens but acts to ensure that these problems are under control and will be solved.
The previous Government was in charge of the destiny of Canadians for nearly 20 years. In charge is perhaps a bit exaggerated. The previous Government wanted to be popular and fell in with the fashion at the time which was to live for the here and now. We have experienced the disastrous consequences of this laissez-aller approach in all social and economic sectors of our society. Many of the problems we are having today, and the debt is the most crucial one, are the result of those years of carelessness and neglect. The Liberal era was a time of instant gratification, of disposable just about everything which created the concept of planned obsolescence.
As approaches go it was not reprehensible, except that in management terms, the cricket's philosophy, as opposed to the ant's, left Canada without any room to manoeuvre when it was necessary to pull back. It is of course much easier to hand out presents and say yes than to ask people to be prudent and to say no. However, there comes a day when we have to choose between being popular and being responsible. Anyone who is
May 11, 1989

responsible for raising children knows this, and anyone who is responsible for making others go the extra mile know this as well. Unfortunately, the previous Government took the easy way out and decided to try and please everyone. As the saying goes, however, gouvemer c'est prevoir. And considering the statistics, I think we have every right to blame our predecessors for poor planning .
Public debt has existed in Canada since Confederation. But it has grown too big in the last 20 years. Borrowing per se is not bad. Canadian consumers borrow to pay for houses, education, cars. Companies borrow to build new factories and buy raw materials to make their products. Governments also borrow to pay for social programs such as unemployment insurance or health insurance, to finance megaprojects like space research or the development of the Old Port of Montreal, to pay public servants' salaries or to heat the Parliament Buildings. Governments also borrow to invest in the future through scientific research and development as well as to subsidize companies and thus promote economic growth. In itself, borrowing is a useful, if not necessary, economic tool, as anyone who has a credit card knows.
However, when expenses are greater than revenues and the money borrowed cannot be repaid within a certain period, a deficit is created. This is called living beyond one's means. Accumulated deficits make up the debt and when we have to borrow to pay the interest, without even being able to repay the principal, we know that the situation is dramatic.
The Government last had a budget surplus in 1969-70. Since 1970-71, the federal Government has spent more every year than it took in. In short, the Government has run a deficit every year and to make up for this shortfall, it has had to borrow. This is normal during tough economic times, but why has the Government continued to spend more than it took in when the economy was going well?
In hindsight, the Government has been too eager in periods of prosperity to satisfy the desires and demands for new services and programs. The previous Liberal Government has too often consented to the creation of new programs or tax shelters instead of resisting it. Short-term needs have sometimes prevailed over longterm consequences. Since 1984, our Government has made an all-out effort to correct the situation. But, Mr. Speaker, the fact remains that loans contracted over 20 years translate into a colossal debt that keeps getting
The Budget-Mrs. Gibeau
bigger. At the end of last month, annual deficits accumulated over the last 20 years had brought the public debt up to $320 billion. As the debt was growing, so was the proportion of public funds used to service it. Last year alone, interest on the debt amounted to $33 billion.
In a way, the debt has reached a critical point. This year, Government revenues from taxes and other sources will finance all our economic and social programs, national defence, as well as our international commitments. But, Mr. Speaker, the crucial point is this: every dollar borrowed by the Government, and probably a little more, is used to pay interest on the public debt. In other words, we are not even paying back the capital. We are simply borrowing to pay more and more interest on the debt. You don't have to be a financial genius to figure out that a person who must borrow money to pay interest to his bank is not in good financial shape.
You know as well as I do that the $33 billion used to pay interest could be better spent elsewhere. That amount represents twice what is spent on elderly benefits, three times what is spent on national defence, 20 times what is spent on job creation and training and 24 times what is spent on all regional development programs. Seen in this light, debt charges bring us to a sad conclusion. Debt interest payments do not in any way contribute to the improvement of Canadians' living standards. The debt problem got worse, but it is the result of 20 years of a spendthrift Government. From the beginning of its first mandate, the Progressive Conservative Government has made fiscal responsability one of its priorities and that has not changed.
Over the past four years we have severely restricted program expenditures and they are now less than the revenue we collect.
As I pointed out earlier, a key element of our progress has been a renewed and systematic effort to eliminate waste and boost public service efficiency. For example- and I draw this to the attention of my colleague on the other side who made unfounded remarks a moment ago-more than 10,000 public service jobs have been eliminated. Operating expenses have been reduced in all departments, productivity has gone up, and that is just the beginning. A number of corporate grants have been cut down or eliminated altogether. Many tax loopholes which were a boon to companies and high income individuals have been closed. A minimum tax has been

May 11, 1989
The Budget-Mrs. Gibeau
implemented to improve the personal income tax system.
Program expenditures which accounted for 19 per cent of national revenues four years ago were brought down to less than 17 per cent last year.
Lower expenditures and higher revenues enabled us to slow down the growth in the public debt. In 1984-85 the debt was going up at the annual rate of 24 per cent. Last year we brought that rate down to 10 per cent. But, given the size of the current debt-$320 billion-the growth rate is still to steep.
All things considered, financial responsibility combined with the implementation of constructive economic policies have strengthened the economy. Our approach is producing results. Canada's economic growth since 1984 ranks among the best of all industrialized nations. Investment growth has been strong. Nearly one and a half million new jobs have been created. Generally speaking, Canadians have enjoyed a much greater economic security.
The Budget proposed by the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is a turning point for Canada's future. It recognizes that our lifestyle is being threatened and this Government has started to effectively and courageously meet that threat.
This Government is taking its responsibilities. The Bourassa people, when voting for the Conservative Party, asked us to protect the quality of their present and future life, as well as Canada's reputation among our economic and social partners.
The Budget put forward by the Minister of Finance aims at protecting our generous social programs, our high standard of living, our markets in a sovereign country that is respected abroad, our inheritance made vulnerable by the ups and downs of interest rates. The challenging measures in the Budget reflect the seriousness of the situation. Some tough decisions had to be taken, but this is what the people elected us for. This Government opted for balanced measures, reflecting regional characteristics and requiring more from those who are in a better position to contribute. We succeeded in greatly reducing program expenditures, after reviewing them to ensure that we get the maximum results from taxpayers' money.
In the Budget, this Government was mainly concerned with people and families. The Government is injecting more money into direct income support for Canadians, more than for any other program.
I would like to tell my constituents in Bourassa that Canadians 65 and over are eligible for old age security pensions, and families with dependent children under 18 are eligible for family allowance payments, regardless of the need for assistance. Those benefits are subject to personal income tax.
The Budget proposes to recover those payments from high- income Canadians. They will refund OAS and family allowance benefits at a rate of 15 per cent of individual net income excluding $50,000.
Repayments will be calculated on the income tax return and will be deductible in determining the amount of income subject to personal income tax. The $50,000 threshold ensures that only benefits received by higher-income Canadians will be subject to repayment. Lower-and middle-income Canadians in receipt of these benefits will not be affected. And of course, we are talking about a net income of $50,000.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) recently announced a new labour force strategy for the 1990s. It will based upon consultation with the private sector to design programs to train Canadians and upgrade their skills so that they can better meet the demands of the quickly evolving labour market.
Expenditures will not be reduced. The size of the unemployment insurance program will remain, but it will be a better program.
In December 1987, the Government announced a national strategy for child care, which consists of new tax assistance to families with pre-school children and children with special needs, and a fund to support innovative initiatives to meet child care needs. The new tax assistance measures are in place, and before the end of its term of office, the Government will act to meet its child care objectives.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had the courage to make the decisions that were necessary. Our Government has acted responsibly. However, the Government is elected by the people, with whom it forms a partnership. The debt is a national problem, and

the success of these measures depends on the understanding and commitment of all Canadians. Only if it is prepared to make such a commitment will our country be able to continue to afford the social, cultural and economic programs that are the very expression of our personality as a nation.
By what we do, we can ensure that our children's opportunities will be unrestricted. We have a duty to pass on to them the same advantages that we inherited and especially, to offer them the province of a better future.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was amazed while listening to the Hon. Member. I was amazed because time and time again the Hon. Member praised the Minister who, in the reality of this world, we can say took the Canadian public and stuck it to them.
I am wondering how the Hon. Member could be proud to be part of a Government which, in 1984, said: "Do not worry about it. We will not touch them, they are a sacred trust". In 1985 Members of that Government had to back off. In 1988 they said the same thing: "We have every nickel accounted for-every little nickel".
Members opposite have called our Leader a liar.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am saying, will the real liar please stand up. Of course, lo and behold who rises-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are walking on thin ice.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In today's paper the Government is quoted as saying: "Jobs, jobs, jobs". In an article in the same newspaper it states that free trade is the culprit in the closure of Toro Co. Ltd.'s only Canadian plant in Manitoba. "The Minnesota-based Toro announced Wednesday it is closing the plant, which opened in 1985 after receiving $720,000 in government aid."
Another article in today's newspaper states:
Canadian auto parts maker Galtaco Inc. is closing its doors in
Canada, affecting about 400 workers -
In Orillia about 260 people will lose their jobs at the same company.
The Budget-Mrs. Gibeau
How can the Hon. Member stand and say that she is proud of her Government? Members opposite should be ashamed of themselves. Not only are they willing to put in place a national sales tax without consulting the provinces, but they say: "If you do not like it we will go ahead and do it alone". As if the national sales tax that the Minister of Finance wants to bring in is not bad enough, he leaked the Budget also. That sales tax will cost the average person thousands of dollars every year. The average person who goes to McDonald's for breakfast will have to pay an extra 40 cents. It costs $5 for a decent breakfast. Now it will cost him $5.40.
Members of the Government state that they have created 1.4 million jobs. Yet those jobs pay only $3.50 per hour.
I have one question to ask of the Hon. Member. How can she stand up to say: "I am proud of my Government"? How can she stand up to say that she is proud when jobs are being lost?
I am wondering if people in my riding are not different from the people in her riding.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are the people in my riding stupid? I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, my riding was represented previously by a Conservative Member of Parliament. Do you know what they did to him? They kicked him out. I am wondering when the people of Canada will do the same to this Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member of the Opposition for giving me this opportunity to say how proud I am of our Government and how proud I am of our Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). I am very proud to be a part of a Government that has both the courage to identify serious problems and the courage to propose solutions.
Mr. Speaker, I have the figures here, and I will read them in English because I think the Hon. Member did not quite understand what I said. I suppose he doesn't speak the language. It says here:

One million, four hundred and thirty-two thousand jobs have been created in the 54 months since September, 1984, including 247,000 in the past year. In contrast

May 11, 1989
The Budget-Mr. Whittaker
only 358,000 jobs were created under the Liberals in the 55 months between February, 1980 and 1984. That is three, almost four times the number of jobs. Since September, 1984, jobs have been created at an average rate of 26,519 a month as compared to the Liberal monthly average of 6,509.

Mr. Speaker, that is why I am proud of our Government, and it makes me furious to see the Opposition deceiving Canadians with their half-truths. They take facts and they twist them, treating their fellow citizens as if they were unable to face reality. The people who elected you, the people who elected us-our fellow Canadians-have a right to know the facts about their country's debt and their country's finances, and our Government has the courage to give them that information so that they will understand and support the courageous measures we are taking.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Hovdebo) on a question or comment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member on her presentation. I would like to comment and ask a question. The most chilling part of this particular Budget is the fact that over the years, even as the Government has reduced the Public Service by, as it suggests, 10,000 jobs, there have been massive increases in taxation. It has had made massive program cuts and it is proud of them, it says. The deficit has gone up by about $1 billion to $31.5 billion. The accumulated debts, if we are to understand the Auditor General, have risen to $340 billion or $350 billion. Interest rates have gone up as well. This Government is keeping them up. We are told that a 1 per cent reduction in interest rates would reduce the deficit by $1.5 billion.
I would like the Hon. Member to defend the Government's policy of keeping the interest rates high.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my Hon. colleague must know that interest rates are not solely dictated by the Bank of Canada. We must borrow on world markets to
make our interest payments and that is exactly why our Government is presenting a Budget that will enable us not only to reduce our deficit but also eventually our debt in order ot protect our country from variations in interest rates. That is why we presented a tough and demanding but certainly very courageous Budget which protects people first, as I said earlier, by making sure that the people who benefit from our programs are those who need them the most.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to get up and speak on any Bill, but in particular I am pleased to be able to speak on a measure as important as the one presently before the House. I am always awed by the surroundings and the history that this place brings to me, and I am astounded by this Government and the measure that is before us at the present time.
I am astounded because throughout the last election we were told who would be the best Party to manage the economy into the future. It has been proven, I would
May 11, 1989

suggest through this Budget, that it is certainly not the Government that sits on that side of the House.
It is certainly not the Government and the Finance Minister (Mr. Wilson) and this Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who are going to lead Canada into the economic future on their white chargers. I would suggest that this Budget is nothing but a blueprint for failure.
I point to a recent Globe and Mail article which quotes the Conference Board of Canada. It states that the federal Budget could bring Canada close to a recession by the end of this year, and will virtually guarantee no economic growth during the rest of 1989.
Calling the Budget inflationary, the Conference Board chief economist, James Frank, said that job losses and larger taxes from the Budget will reduce personal disposable income by $5 billion next year, in large part through the $2.2 billion that will be collected in additional personal taxes.
That is the blueprint for the future. The Government has brought down a Budget on the backs of the small wage earners, on the backs of small business, on the backs of agriculture, on the backs of the unemployed, on the backs of the pensioners, and it expects us to believe that it is the saviour of the economic future of Canada. Nonsense. It has shown where its priorities are.
A question raised earlier by my colleague suggests that the Finance Minister back in 1985 told us that there were not enough rich. I would suggest that this Budget shows part of that agenda, that he is trying to create more rich on the backs of the poor. I suggest that we in Canada will not stand for it. We in this comer of the House will not stand for it. We intend to show those people in Canada exactly what you, the Government, is doing to them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What you did to Manitoba.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are not kissing them before you are creating the problem.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Your record is good.
The Budget-Mr. Whittaker

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I might, for a minute, now that I have awakened the Member, I would like to talk a little bit about how this Budget will affect my area.
When I read the Budget I thought about my area, Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt, and what it has. I looked at the tax increases, the two per cent increase in the federal surtax, a 15 per cent hike in unemployment insurance premiums, increases in sales and excise taxes. I understand that will pull hundreds of dollars out of taxpayers' pockets. I looked to see how they will benefit by these tax increases.
Instead, what did I find? I found a one per cent cut-back in health and welfare payments, cuts in co-op and rental housing, cuts in regional development, cuts in child care, cuts to VIA, cuts in the tourism budget, proposed cuts to crop insurance, cuts to the Federal Business Development Bank. I looked to see what was missing. There was nothing for the environment or the infrastructure so badly needed by municipalities. Then I looked to see how this will affect my area and what will be directly affected.
In the Boundary country and in the Merritt-Princeton area we have a major mining industry. I looked in the Budget and found out, yes, there are cuts there too. There are cuts to the mining exploration development area. We have forestry in Grand Forks, Midway, Greenwood, Okanagan Falls, Penticton, Princeton, and Merritt. Through these cuts I find that, yes, my areas will be hit by cuts to reforestation and cuts to regional expansion. I looked further and saw agriculture which is one of the major industries in the Okanagan part of the riding. There is nothing in the Budget to help the agricultural industry. In fact, there are major cuts once again.
There are cuts proposed to the stabilization programs and there is nothing to assist small business to produce value added products. My friend says that it is a show- and I suggest that that is correct-of harmonization under the Free Trade Agreement once again.
What is there in my area that will really be affected aside from that? Tourism is of major importance. I spoke to the Chamber of Commerce in Penticton recently. I was told that the Okanagan area has over two million tourists a year who visit and spend well over $88 million, representing 50 per cent to 60 per cent of direct and indirect hospitality jobs. Of these almost 20 per cent are tourists from the United States, Japan, Europe, and other countries. This industry will be directly affected by the $10 million in cut-backs to the tourism budget, $10

May 11, 1989
The Budget-Mr. Whittaker
million that prior had been set out for advertising and for the pursuit of tourist dollars from abroad. We are losing that under this Budget. In an area where tourism is so crucial, I suggest that that is totally unacceptable to the people of my area and certainly to the people of British Columbia who depend on tourism to a great extent for their incomes.
It surprises me again seeing this Government cutting back on the tourism budget when, as a member of the regional board of Okanagan-Similkameen, we recognized how important tourism was to our area and set aside some budget for advertising to ensure that people knew about our area.
Yet, what do we have? Instead of cutting back on the $10 million plus which the Government is spending on advertising to push some of the other programs which it cannot sell to the people and spending that money where it can be used, it is spending money on nonsense such as advertising this Budget which is indefensible. That money should be used in the tourism budget where it would create employment and productivity within our communities. It would take the people off the unemployment rolls which, incidentally, in my area are over twice the national average.
This Government, after diddling with the GATT, the Free Trade Agreement and agriculture, is now nailing coffins by pulling money out of the tourism budget. That, in our region, is unacceptable, totally unacceptable. We will fight for our rights and for the tourism budget. We will not accept without a fight what the Government is doing to the area of Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt and the Boundary country.
I would like now to speak about small business. The small business area recognized by Statistics Canada as having created 70 per cent of all employment between 1980 and 1988. What has this Government done to assist small business, to recognize the contribution which the small business community has given to Canada since Confederation, but particularly in the last eight years? The Government has now put the unemployment insurance on the backs of the employer and employee. The Government has stepped out of the unemployment insurance program where it should be to ensure that it continues. This is another step in the harmonization of
the Free Trade Agreement. The Government is looking to please the Americans instead of looking after what we have and what we should be looking after in this country.
What else did the small business person get? The Federal Business Development Bank has helped a little bit-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A mighty little bit.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-although it seems to look to larger business for loans. The one program that is of benefit to small business is the provision of advice on management services. I had occasion on the weekend to refer a small business person to the FBDB for that specific service.
What do we find in this Budget? A cut of $13 million out of the management service area of the Federal Business Development Bank. The one area in that bank that actually helps small business.
The small businessman often is a person without many skills who wants to be his own boss. He needs that assistance. He needs all the help that he can get. He needs someone to turn to. That service has been offered by the Federal Business Development Bank and has been suggested as a service to be added to the Farm Credit Corporation, to assist farmers in setting up their businesses.
What have we got? We have the small businessman getting the shaft once again from the Government which says it is the friend of small business. I suggest that the Government is not the friend of small business. It has been shown time and again that the agenda is a large corporate agenda which we have seen from year to year since 1984, and it is the agenda that is again before us now.
I saw with interest a recent story in The Financial Post which said that small firms may be hardest hit with the implementation of the new tax. It points out a number of things that have been of some concern to me when looking at how the tax changes will affect small business. It deals with accounts receivable for service industries and refers particularly to advertising agencies, but could also refer to lawyers, accountants and computer outfits that offer services to the public. When those companies bill for their services, they must add the 9 per cent service tax under the proposed value added tax the
May 11, 1989

Government has given notice it will bring in, and they must then remit that to the federal Government.
What happens when a small businessman has to write that off? He has to come up with that money when he bills for his services. There is not much room built in for him to defer because he is penalized. He has to come up with the money. I can tell Hon. Members, as one who has worked for small businesses, that a small business person with a marginal corporation cannot afford that extra $5,000 or $8,000. In small towns such as those I represent, he would need that money to keep his business going. He would need that money to feed and clothe his children and to pay his mortgage.
The Government does not care, I suggest, for the small business person. The Government cares only for its corporate friends.
The article also points out that probably hardest hit will be Canadian magazines which are already reporting flat incomes this year. They will have to charge tax on subscriptions which are very price sensitive. This is another example of the Government threatening a part of our culture as it did through the Free Trade Agreement.
There is one hope. The final paragraph of the article says that Saul Muskat, a Toronto accountant, points out that it is creating a whole new specialized industry. There will be a lot more work for accountants and tax lawyers. That is not good enough for those of us who care for average Canadians. We want a Budget that is fair to everyone. We want a Government that will tax large corporations and have them pay their fair share. We want a Government that will recognize that there are others in Canada than large corporate entities and wealthy land owners and employers. We want the Government to recognize that there are many of us in Canada who do not make a lot of money and who cannot afford to pay the extra taxes and have the added cut-backs.
If I might, I would move on to pensions for seniors. In 1988, the Prime Minister was quoted as saying:
Let me say a special word to the senior citizens.
The Budget-Mr. Whittaker
He said this in Summerside, Prince Edward Island, an area that he has now shafted once again. He said:
-in the future Canada will be doing more, not less, for all of you. As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada, social benefits, especially those for the elderly, will be improved, not diminished, by our government which -is committed to social justice and fairness for Canadians.
Well, what did we get this time? We got some of that social justice. We got some of that fairness for seniors. Once again, as it did in 1985, the Government is attacking the universality of social programs, just as it was predicted it would do during the election campaign and during the debate over the Free Trade Agreement. It is part of the harmonization process, as much of this Budget is. It is an outright attack on seniors and social programs. I say to the Government, shame on you.
Back in 1985, the National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation led a fight against the Government when it attacked the old age security. Once again, this organization is starting to mount an attack, and I add my voice of support to that group. There is an article in The Ottawa Citizen today which points out that the federation is shocked that the Government is shaking the underpinnings of the Canadian social safety net.
Les Batterson, the federation president, says that they think they have been betrayed because both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance indicated that there would be no tampering with social security programs and that seniors were misled by statements that were made during the election.
I feel sorry for Mrs. Mulroney. I know she is a woman beyond criticism. The only criticism I might have is that she should teach her son that he should pay a little more attention to the truth. It appears that he has been a stranger to that recently. We saw how he reacted once he proceeded to tell seniors what he would do for them. He has done it, but he did not do what he said he would do.

Once again, during the election campaign and over the prior four years, the Government told us it would look after the women of Canada. What has been done? I want to say to the Government that it had better review what it has done in this Budget and look at what we as Canadians need. It had better look at the management of the future and come to conclusions other than the ones reached in the Budget.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on the speech made by the Hon. Member for Okanagan- Similkameen-Merritt. I am very concerned about some of the things the Hon. Member has said. I suppose I am really concerned about his lack of interest in giving credit to the people of the tourism industry. He feels that they cannot promote their businesses on their own and that there should be all sorts of federal money going toward advertising the tourism business in British Columbia. Certainly the tourism business in Ontario has been doing a fine job. These free enterprisers and entrepreneurs have attracted people to their places of business and feel good about it. He feels there has to be all sorts of federal money going to it and that the federal Government has not done right by small business. He also suggested that we have not assisted small business.
The Hon. Member said that he worked in small business, but small business people have told us in the last four and a half years when visiting Parliament Hill that they would like to have the opportunity to be unfettered, not hemmed in, or told what to do by government. They would like to go their own way.
Also local communities have told us that individual communities like to have flexibility in their decision making with respect to how best to help small business develop in their own areas. That is being accomplished by the funds that are being directed toward the Communities Futures. The Government feels positive about this and has had a good record in this regard.
Certainly the change in UI funds can be redirected to creating jobs, most especially through the Communities Futures Program, an excellent program. Small business told those of us on the DRIE committee during 1984, 1985, 1986 and 1987 when they appeared before us that they needed that kind of flexibility. We listened to what they had to say. Perhaps the Member should go out and have a talk with the small business people.
I think it is a shame that the Member tends to confuse the issue in connection with the higher income pensioners paying back some of their Old Age Security. It certainly goes on above $50,000, which is certainly a credible amount of money to be made each year. I do not think that he should be confused. If one has $100,000 income in 1989, one will only be paying $700 of that money back. I think the record should be kept clear in that regard.
Earlier the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands tended to confuse the issue. I do not think it was intentional on the part of the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands or the Member from Okanagan, but I think the record should be made clear. It goes along with what the socialists seem to have been saying for some period of time, that high income people should be paying their fair share. In the situation faced by higher income people, along with having the universality of the program maintained, they will pay back to assist in this terrible deficit and long-term debt problem in Canada. The Member should take note of that and be careful that he speaks clearly, concisely, and accurately about such things.
May 11, 1989

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be given the opportunity to reply. What I have heard over the last six days of budget debate involves some confusion on the government benches as opposed to those of the Opposition.
Perhaps my friend has missed the point of some of what was said not only by myself but by some of the other Members on this side of the House with respect to tourism and small business.
I have spoken over the last week and a half with many of the people involved in the tourism and small business industries in my area. I am not getting the same type of feedback as that which the Hon. Members gives the House. I am little surprised that he would tell me that, given the fact that throughout the course of time and through the lobby by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business Mr. Bulloch was constantly warning the Government about its plan for a value added tax and what it would do to small business.
In meeting with the hospitality industry people in my area just last week, a number of concerns were raised including unemployment insurance and how that was going to affect small business people. Concerns were raised over the lack of government interest in the tourism industry. On the one hand under Bill C-3 it would say that it was going to set up all these wonderful things for tourism. Then, a week later in the Budget, it slashed $10 million from the tourism promotion part of the Budget. Those are some of the concerns about which the people in my area have talked to me.
In speaking about the claw-back provision, I make very clear that I understand it. I want to ensure that the government benches understand. Government Members have set it at $50,000 this year, but what is going to happen next year? They have now booted the door open to universality. They have set their toe in and they are intending, I would submit, to blast it wide open with that one little thrust, saying that it really does not count because it is the higher income earners we are getting at. Nonsense; it is part of a larger agenda of harmonization.
They are going to knock it down as the Government, $40,000 in years to come or $10,000? What is the limit going to be? Is it now going to become a total phase out of our social security programs? It is only a start. It is that possibility to which we are objecting, and we are flagging
The Budget-Mr Whittaker
it so that the people of Canada will know that it is the start of what is to come.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have a comment, Mr. Speaker. It seems that all sides of the House, speaker after speaker, have acknowledged the fact that we do have a deficit and we do have to address it.
The difference is how we address the issue of the deficit. The Liberal Party believes that to address the deficit we have to concentrate on increased productivity.
I would like to bring to the attention of the Members of the House that Canada is one of the leading countries when it comes to export of raw material. Unfortunately we are nowhere when it comes to areas of high technology areas, or when it comes to many other areas such as our investment in education, illiteracy and so on. While we are one of the largest importers of wood, we still import saws from Italy in order to cut wood. We have a very strong mining industry and we ship to Japan, Hong Kong and elsewhere, we still import the machinery in order to dig and do such things
We have spoken about the tourism industry. Yes, it is a service industry. Unfortunately in this country, we still seem to be putting a lot of emphasis on the service sector rather than concentrating on the manufacturing end of it.
A Japanese speaker who was in this country a couple of weeks ago said that Canada, in order to be on the leading edge in every area, would have to concentrate more on manufacturing. There is no way that we can get out of this situation, unless we spend more money in the area of research and development and education and make manufacturing a priority of this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree totally. Valued added products must be given priority within Canada, across the nation. We can no longer accept that we are primary industry people who ship out our products for manufacture. We have to look further into what we are doing and encourage that type of investment.
Part of the education and research funds that we have spoken about in other Bills are so important that they bring back enormous dividends to our country which we can certainly use in the future in the value added areas of our manufacturing, as well as in making Canada known throughout the world as not only a good research

May 11, 1989
The Budget-Mr. Vien
country but as the best country to which to go for research.

speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Laurentides (Mr. Vien).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am greatful for this opportunity to make my maiden speech in this House.
First of all, I wish to very sincerely thank the people of my beautiful riding of Laurentides for their trust on November 21st.
Since 1984, Mr. Speaker, the solid economic record of our Government fully demonstrates the soundness of its policies. We have created a million and a half new jobs and our economy has witnessed a quicker expansion than those of most other industrialized countries. We have achieved these goals together, both as a Government and as a nation, because we have been able to make difficult choices and to take stringent measures to deal with our economic and financial problems.
However, Mr. Speaker, these achievements are now being threatened by growing inflationary pressures both here and abroad.
As the result of these pressures, short-term interest rates are rising; they are higher today than we generally expected them to be hardly a few months ago. Early in 1988, most economic forecasters had predicted that the impact of the October 1987 krach would slow down the economic growth of industrialized nations to more sustainable levels. None of these forecasters had predicted the rapid growth and inflationary pressures which have been recorded in Canada and in other major industrialized nations.
Economic growth has been very strong, and Canada and countries abroad had to tighten their monetary policies to curb this inflation.
Failure to act now will result in a greater threat to our economic stability due to greater inflationary pressures and higher interest rates which could lead us in to a recession.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has recognized that many Canadians are frustrated by the
increase in interest rates. Some are even suggesting that the Government should order the Bank of Canada to lower them. But interest rates move in relation to other economic factors, and therefore cannot be dealt with independently.
Mr. Speaker, inflationary pressures are responsible for high interest rates. To attack the symptoms instead of the causes would not solve the problem.
And we will not succeed in controlling inflation by increasing the money supply. Rampant inflation always brings about higher interest rates. Such inflationary spiral is a recipe for economic disaster.
Mr. Speaker, the Government will not make that mistake. Let us not forget the inflationary outburst and explosion in interest rates of the early eighties.
The erosion of confidence in the economy, the collapse of growth and employment in all regions of Canada and above all the immeasurable damage done to millions of Canadians.
As the Finance Minister said, he expects inflation and interest rates to slow down in the mid term. This will allow the economy to grow on average at its potential rate of 3 per cent between 1991 and 1994. But that potential growth rate will not be reached automatically.
Mr. Speaker, we must put in place firm, moderate and coherent budgetary and monetary measures that will keep us in the right direction, to bring down inflation and interest rates and prevent them from rising again. We must follow a realistic and responsible policy in which the short-and medium term-risks are well balanced.
Through its Budget, the Government is seeking to guarantee the future and not mortgage it. That is why the Budget comes firmly to grips with the main obstacle between us and that future: the problem of an increasing debt.
The measures in this Budget reflect the seriousness of the debt problem we are facing. We also tried to make sure the whole package was balanced, took into account regional considerations and fell more heavily on those most able to bear it.
Mr. Speaker, as a Government, we are acting with determination to reduce expenditures and to improve our efficiency and our operations. We also ask to all

Canadians to take a large part in solving this national problem.
We have adopted expenditure reductions affecting a wide variety of programs, from national defence to government operations. When fully implemented, these reductions will amount to $2.5 billion a year. As a result of these measures and those announced previously, program expenditures will continue to decrease significantly. By 1993-94, they will have fallen to their lowest level in a quarter of a centuiy.
Although expenditure reductions contribute significantly to meeting the Budget objectives, we also had to increase revenues.
Mr. Speaker, these measures have also been designed to weigh more heavily on those taxpayers who can afford to contribute more. The raises have been distributed in a balanced way among several sources of revenue: corporate and individual income tax, sales taxes and unemployment insurance funding. On the other hand, measures such as the doubling of the refundable sales tax credit mean we can guarantee that low-income Canadians will pay the smallest share of the tax burden.

The Government introduced the refundable sales tax credit in 1986, and has expanded the credit since then. In this Budget the Government is doubling the tax credits for adults and children. By 1990 these credits will be $140 per adult, and $70 per child.
In addition, in 1990 the income threshold up to which the full credit is provided will be raised from $16,000 to $18,000. This means that an individual with a net income of $18,000 or less will receive $140. A couple with two children would receive $420.
For the 1990 taxation year the extended credit will provide $655 million in support to lower-income Canadians. This will more than compensate recipients for the full credit for the federal sales tax increase announced in the Budget.
When the Government undertakes sales tax reform in the near future, it will be introducing a new goods and services sales tax credit that will involve a major expansion of benefits. It means that even if individuals do not pay income tax they will receive the credit in a cheque from the Government. Payments will be made regularly every three months, the first one in advance of the start-up of the new system on January 1, 1991. Lower
The Budget-Mr. Vien
and modest-income households will be better off as a result of sales tax reform.
Other tax changes to benefit middle-income households will be introduced as well. In combination, the new tax credit and other tax changes will result in a more progressive system. The Government's goal is to ensure that families earning less than $30,000 a year will be better off as a result of our sales tax reform.
[Translation}
Mr. Speaker, the tax on goods and services will benefit Canadians in all regions of the country. In fact, implementation of the goods and services tax will result in a fairer tax system, once sales tax reform is a reality, thanks to the new credit for the goods and services tax and the lowering of income tax. The Government's objective is to ensure that all these measures will leave families earning less than $30,000 a year better off once the goods and services tax is in place.
The goods and services tax will improve our international competitiveness considerably. Our export industries will be better placed, while Canadian companies will be on an equal footing with importers. It will strengthen our economy, which will attract more investors and create more jobs. A modem tax base, generating stable revenues, will help the government reduce the deficit and offer Canadians the programs they want.
The overall effect of these budgetary measures will exceed $5 billion this year and will total $9 billion next year. This year, these measures will almost compensate for the increase in interest rates and will leave the deficit at $30.5 billion. Next year, the deficit will be reduced to $28 billion, and the debt will stop growing faster than the economy. That is an important result, Mr. Speaker.
The Budget will enable us to cut the annual deficit in half, bringing it down to $15 billion by 1993-1994. As the deficit diminishes, the debt will use up a lesser proportion of our national income and interest payments will take up a lesser portion of each tax dollar.
Mr. Speaker, nobody likes tax increases. Yet the debt is a major problem because we have not yet paid in full the cost of government programs. Before 1984, successive governments had acted in such a way as to reduce the tax base. This resulted in a lack of fairness and a reduction in federal revenues.
Mr. Speaker, this government has since then taken steps to restore the integrity of the tax system. Over the last four years, we have taken a number of steps, through the budgets or otherwise, to eliminate certain tax concessions, to plug loopholes and to restrict the possibility of

May 11, 1989
The Budget-Mr. Vien
tax avoidance for corporations and upper income individuals. We have also reduced the incentives to tax avoidance through a comprehensive reform which widens the tax base and lowers tax rates.
These initiatives have transformed the tax system in a more equitable and reliable source of revenues, thus ensuring that we get the funds necessary to preserve the future of Canada. The budget reflects the seriousness of our situation. We have made difficult choices. We have tried to ensure that the budget measures are balanced, that they take into account regional variations and that they impose the heaviest burden on those who are better able to support it.
